title: Turn Any Book Into an AI Skill You'll Actually Use
author: Vicky Zhao
summary: Argues that the standard way of turning a book into an AI skill fails through compounding abstraction: the author already abstracted lived experience into a book, a summary strips the nuance and worked examples, and asking an LLM to distil that summary into a skill is an abstraction of an abstraction of an abstraction — which is why the resulting skill comes out vague and average. Since AI is good at digesting volume, feed it rich source context rather than a compressed one-pager. A skill only earns its place if it does three things: knows the specific situation that triggers it, drives an actual behaviour change, and records the result so a feedback loop closes. The deeper claim is that learning has not happened until behaviour changes; remembering a book without changing what you do is "intellectual fantasising".
takeaways: The abstraction problem: experience → book → summary → skill is four levels of abstraction, and nuance is stripped at every step. Give the AI the richest source you have, not a summary.
A useful skill must answer three questions: WHEN to use the method, HOW it changes behaviour, and WHAT happened afterwards (record and review).

Shu-ha-ri, from Japanese martial arts and tea ceremony, is the mastery ladder: shu = follow the master's method exactly, ha = explore and push the edges of the framework, ri = build your own from accumulated experience.
Most people fail by skipping shu and trying to do all three levels at once — customising a method before they have any evidence about whether it works.
Zhao's own worked example: she used Allan Dib's One-Page Marketing Plan as a base but mixed in what Apple did, customised the parts she was uncomfortable with, and got nowhere.
Treat it like a scientific experiment — change one variable at a time, run the expert's method a few times first to establish a baseline before adapting it.
AI's real advantage in learning is emotionless support: learning brushes against ego, uncertainty and fear, and an agent guides the loop without requiring you to stay disciplined and rational.
With agents, context matters far more than prompt craft: "if you use agents as opposed to the chat version... prompt is less important. Context is everything with agents."
quotes: Learning doesn't happen until we change our behavior. So, if the behavior still stays the same, then there was no real learning going on. It was just intellectual fantasizing of a better world.
By the time you're creating your skill, you are taking an abstraction of an abstraction of an abstraction of an idea... So it's not surprising that at the end we get something very average.
AI is really good at digesting information. So we don't want to give it abstraction of abstraction.
What AI is really good at doing is doing emotionless support. And that is crucial, right? Learning is actually a very emotional experience.
If you use agents as opposed to the chat version... prompt is less important. Context is everything with agents.
You're not going to change all the variables at once and try to see if something works or not. You have to change it one at a time.
bestIdeas: Abstraction budget — every compression step between source and system costs nuance. Transfers to any RAG, prompt or documentation pipeline: count the hops and cut them.
A skill is a feedback loop, not a prompt. Situation → method → action → recorded result is what turns advice into learning, and it applies to any system meant to change behaviour.
Shu-ha-ri as a governance rule for adopting frameworks: earn the right to customise with evidence, rather than deciding upfront which parts you like.
Delegate the discipline. Where a practice fails because humans are inconsistent, an agent holding the loop is a structural fix rather than a motivational one.
tools: Codex — used live to build the One-Page Marketing Plan skill from a plain-language prompt.
Claude Code — named as equivalent; the method works in any agent.
Obsidian — the note-taking half of the two setup variants (with notes / without notes).
The One-Page Marketing Plan (Allan Dib) — the worked example book, and its nine-grid framework.
method: Pick the source (book, podcast, video) and the specific behaviour you want to change.
Articulate the SITUATION that should trigger the skill — not "whenever", but a named recurring moment.
Give the agent the richest context available rather than a summary; name the framework so it can ground itself.
Ask it to build a skill that (a) applies the method and (b) records both whether you followed it and what resulted.
Run the expert's method as written — the shu stage — several times before customising anything.
Review the recorded results for patterns, then adapt (ha), and eventually build your own framework (ri).
